units.en: A ⟦0⟧ gets initiated on a specific province between two task forces, one of them being the attacker. This usually happens after a ⟦1⟧ process is complete or opposing fleets move onto the same province. Naval and port strikes by ⟦2⟧ trigger a naval battle that resolves instantly. Otherwise the battle lasts until one side is fully escaped or destroyed. The defender always joins the battle with full efficiency while the attacker may have a reduced efficiency depending on circumstances.
Inside of battles, ships can behave independently and ⟦0⟧, which are normally abstracted, are also present as individual ships.
⟦0⟧: Consists of ⟦1⟧, which screen the battle-line and carrier group from torpedoes.
⟦0⟧: Consists of ⟦1⟧ except for carriers. In addition to providing heavy firepower, these ships screen the carrier group from torpedoes.
⟦0⟧: Consists of carriers which can strike at long range. If any convoys are present, they will also appear in this area.
⟦0⟧: Consists of ⟦1⟧, which may threaten the enemy battle-line and carrier group if they are insufficiently screened from torpedoes.
Reference HOI4 Dev Diary - New Naval Combat "Battle-lines" Forum:1133625

The ratio of screen ships to ⟦0⟧ and convoys is the ⟦1⟧. With good positioning, 100% screening efficiency is reached when the ratio is 3⟦2⟧ screen(s) per capital ship and/or carrier and an additional 0.5⟦3⟧ screen(s) per convoy. For example, if you have 4 carriers and 4 battleships, you need 24 screen ships in order to reach 100% screening efficiency, or if you have 16 convoys under attack from submarines, you need 8 screen ships to reach 100% screening efficiency. High screening efficiency prevents enemy torpedo attacks against the battle-line and carrier groups, and confers the following bonuses to those groups:
Hit chance: up to ⟦0⟧ at 100% screening efficiency
Retreat speed: up to ⟦0⟧ at 100% screening efficiency

The ratio of capital ships to carriers and convoys is the ⟦0⟧. With good positioning, 100% carrier screening efficiency is reached when the ratio is 1⟦1⟧ capital ship(s) per carrier and an additional 0.25⟦2⟧ capital ship(s) per convoy. High carrier screening efficiency further prevents enemy torpedo attacks against the carrier group (stacking diminishingly). It also provides confers the following bonuses to carriers and convoys:
Sortie efficiency: up to ⟦0⟧ at 100% carrier screening efficiency
Retreat speed: up to ⟦0⟧ at 100% carrier screening efficiency

Bad positioning applies a penalty to how much ships contribute to both screening efficiency and carrier screening efficiency. The penalty increases linearly up to ⟦0⟧ at 0% positioning. This may increase the screening ratio required to achieve 100% efficiency by up to ⟦1⟧.
Heavy attack guns and light attack guns can fire every 1⟦0⟧ hour(s) and 1⟦1⟧ hour(s), respectively. Torpedoes normally fire every 4⟦2⟧ hours. When This can be reduced by ⟦3⟧ with the ⟦4⟧ trait.

Each ship with offensive weapons (i.e. not carriers and convoys) and whose weapons are on cooldown can target three enemy ships, independently, per combat hour; one with its depth charges/light weapons, one with torpedoes, and one with heavy guns. Depending on weapon type and enemy screening, only certain enemy groups can be targeted.
⟦0⟧ the only weapon type that can target submarines, and only if they are revealed (see below)
⟦0⟧ can only target the closest non-empty group, though carriers and convoys will not target enemy carriers or convoys
⟦0⟧ can target the first two non-empty groups

⟦0⟧ the probability that a torpedo can target capital ships (bypassing the screening group) is 100%, minus the enemy ⟦1⟧. To target ships in the carrier group (including convoys), it needs to pass an additional check of 100% minus the enemy ⟦2⟧.
Submarines will only target screens when set to High risk engagement rule. They will only target capitals when set to Medium risk or higher.

Out of the remaining valid targets one is chosen by weighted random selection. If the firing ship is not currently running away, the enemies are weighted as follows (numbers in parenthesis for light guns):⟦0⟧

If the target is less than full strength, up to +100% bonus are applied to the weight. If the target is escaping, the weight is reduced by 50%. If the target is actively fighting (i.e. not waiting), a +50% bonus is applied.
The weighting is similar when the firing ship is escaping but only considers targets that are actively fighting and always chooses the highest scoring target, without randomization.

Submarines are completely immune to being targeted while they are hidden. This is indicated by a crossed-out eye symbol over the submarine. Revealing a submarine starts a cooldown of 20⟦0⟧ hours, after which the submarine will hide again (unless the cooldown gets refreshed).
There are three circumstances that reveal submarines:

If the submarine starts the battle on the defending side, it will be initially revealed for 16⟦0⟧ hours. This typically happens when its task force gets ⟦1⟧ by enemy patrols. Due to how low reveal chances are for submarines once they are already in battle, this is the main way that anti-submarine ships, especially anti-submarine carriers using naval bombers, can be effective against submarines. Importantly, ships ⟦2⟧ can never reveal submarines in this way, counterintuitively making anti-submarine ships bad at killing raiding submarines when they are escorting convoys.

If the enemy task force has any ships with sub detection greater than zero, there is a 3.5%⟦0⟧ chance of the submarine revealing itself every time it attacks. The submarine's visibility affects this chance, and bad positioning increases the visibility effect by up to 200%.⟦1⟧ It can be reduced with torpedo reveal chance modifiers, e.g., from the ⟦2⟧ technology, the ⟦3⟧ admiral trait, and submarine naval doctrines like ⟦4⟧ or ⟦5⟧. This is the primary way that submarines are revealed during naval battles, e.g., against convoy escorts. Reducing torpedo reveal chance is therefore very important when using submarines in this role.
If the enemy has any amount of sub detection, then every combat hour, there is a chance for the submarine to get revealed passively by the enemy's sub detection:⟦0⟧

Due to what is likely a mistake in the game's code, the chances of this happening are very small even when using dedicated anti-submarine ships against outdated submarines. For example, with an average sub detection of 45, which is near the theoretical maximum for a task force of only dedicated anti-submarine destroyers, against 25 sub visibility (for unupgraded, outdated Early Submarines), the chance to reveal a hidden submarine every hour is 0.457%. This means it will take on average 152 hours, or about 6.333 days, before a given outdated Early Submarine is passively revealed in combat for the standard 16 hours. Similarly, due to what is probably a mistake, aerial sub detection contributes 0%⟦0⟧ to the chance of passively revealing a submarine in battle, meaning only the sub detection of ships is considered.

The base hit chance for guns and torpedoes is 10%,⟦0⟧ and the base hit chance for depth charges is 11%.⟦1⟧ If the firing ship lacks manpower or organization, their hit chances are reduced by up to ⟦2⟧ and by up to ⟦3⟧, respectively.

This is further modified by the hit profile of both the firing weapon and the target ship. Ships with lower hit profiles are harder to hit, and weapons with lower hit profiles are better at targeting.

This means that a weapon will suffer penalties to hit chance against a ship whose hit profile is smaller than that of the weapon. The hit chance can be modified by bad weather, night, ⟦0⟧, fire control and/or radar ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧ traits and policies (with ⟦3⟧), ⟦4⟧ spirits (with ⟦5⟧), and the ship's ⟦6⟧'s skill level and traits such as ⟦7⟧ and ⟦8⟧. If the hit chance of an attack does not result in a hit, the target remains unaffected.

In practical terms, a speed increase of 4% is roughly equivalent to increasing your ship's effective HP against other ships by about 1%. This increase applies across the board regardless of your ship's sub/surface visibility or what weapon is being used against it. Similarly, a visibility decrease of 1% is roughly equivalent to increasing your ship's effective HP against other ships by about 1.1%.

For example, a 1936 light cruiser with 15 surface visibility and a speed of 32.0 kn has a ship hit profile of ca. 41.7. When fired upon by another 1936 light cruiser with its light cruiser batteries with no other hit chance modifiers besides a basic fire control system, the base hit chance will be 102.5% and the weapon hit profile will be 45, making the final hit chance of the attack ca. 87.9%. If the light cruiser had a ⟦0⟧ surface visibility bonus from, e.g., the ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧ spirit, resulting in a surface visibility of 14.25, it would have a ship hit profile of 39.6, and so the hit chance of this attack from an enemy light cruiser would instead be ca. 79.3%.
Aircraft use entirely different math to figure out their hit chances when naval bombing that ignores the visibility and speed of their targets. See the ⟦0⟧ section for more information.
Armor and piercing can affect both the ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ chance of heavy attack guns and light attack guns.
Torpedoes ignore armor entirely, though some heavier armor modules do reduce incoming ⟦0⟧ from torpedoes and the ⟦1⟧ chance of torpedoes.

The respective weapon type damage of the ship can be modified by doctrines, the ⟦0⟧, the ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧ (if present), and the admiral's skills and traits. Bad positioning can cause a penalty of up to 50%⟦3⟧. The Defense modifier of the enemy admiral's skill level will also reduce the damage.
If the weapon can not pierce the enemy armor, damage is reduced by up to ⟦0⟧. See ⟦1⟧ for more details.
The damage gets randomized with a modifier between ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧.⟦2⟧

Damage is applied against both the target's HP (by 60%⟦0⟧) and organization (by 100%⟦1⟧). Additionally ships start out immune against organization damage, scaling up to the nominal value as the ship's HP level goes down. As an example, assume a ship with 100/50 HP/Org receives multiple hits of 50 damage each. The consecutive hits will do 30/0, 30/15, 30/30, and 30/45 HP/Org damage, with the fourth hit sinking the ship.
A critical hit is a particularly devastating hit against the target which can also damage some of its critical parts. The resulting penalties can only be removed by repairing the ship.

The chance for a torpedo to score a critical hit is 10%.⟦0⟧ For other weapon types the base chance is 5%,⟦1⟧ but also depends on whether the armor can be pierced (see ⟦2⟧) and the target's reliability (scaling down to 0% at 100% reliability).
The ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ traits can each increase and lower critical hit chances, irrespective of weapon type.

If a critical hit does occur, it potentially affects one of the critical parts on the ship. The chance for this is 10%⟦0⟧ for attacks from other ships and 10%⟦1⟧ for aerial attacks, both inversely scaled by reliability (e.g., at 25% reliability the chance increases to 10%÷25%=40%).
